   117		// against it and its result is simply discarded with the old map, rather than
   118		// being observed by anyone after the mutation.
   119		c.byDir = map[string]*remoteSnapshot{}
   120	}
   121	
   122	func cacheFromContext(ctx context.Context) *gitRemoteCache {
   123		c, ok := ctx.Value(gitRemoteCacheKey{}).(*gitRemoteCache)
   124		if !ok {
   125			return nil
   126		}
   127		return c
   128	}
   129	
   130	// gitReadRepo identifies the repository the memoized git reads resolve against,
   131	// and so the cache partition: the context's scoped worktree root when there is
   132	// one, else the repo containing the process working directory that `git` would
   133	// inherit. Returns false when neither can be established, which callers read as
   134	// "do not cache" — an unidentifiable repository must not share another's answers.
   135	//
   136	// The repo root rather than the raw cwd: `git remote get-url` answers the same
   137	// from any subdirectory of a repository, so two calls from different
   138	// subdirectories should share one answer. paths.WorktreeRoot is memoized per cwd,
   139	// so this stays far cheaper than the subprocess it is protecting.
   140	func gitReadRepo(ctx context.Context) (string, bool) {
   141		if root, ok := settings.WorktreeRoot(ctx); ok && root != "" {
   142			return root, true
   143		}
   144		root, err := paths.WorktreeRoot(ctx)
   145		if err != nil || root == "" {
   146			return "", false
   147		}
   148		return root, true
   149	}
   150	
   151	// snapshotFor returns the per-repository snapshot, or nil when this call must not
   152	// be cached. Acquires c.mu for the map access and releases it before returning;
   153	// callers must NOT hold it. The lock is deliberately never held across a git read
   154	// (see gitRemoteCache).
   155	func (c *gitRemoteCache) snapshotFor(ctx context.Context) *remoteSnapshot {
   156		repoRoot, ok := gitReadRepo(ctx)
   157		if !ok {
   158			return nil
   159		}
   160		c.mu.Lock()
   161		defer c.mu.Unlock()
   162		snap := c.byDir[repoRoot]
   163		if snap == nil {
   164			snap = &remoteSnapshot{member: map[string]bool{}}
   165			c.byDir[repoRoot] = snap
   166		}
   167		return snap
   168	}
   169	
   170	// cachedRemotesInConfigOrder returns the memoized remote list for this call's
   171	// repository, computing it via read on a miss. Without a cache installed, or when
   172	// the repository cannot be established, it just calls read.
   173	//
   174	// A read that FAILS is never memoized. read reports "no remotes" and "could not
   175	// tell" as distinct outcomes precisely so this can hold: caching a failure's empty
   176	// list would turn one transient git hiccup into a process-long "this repo has no
   177	// remotes", and the election answers that by silently skipping checkpoint sync.
   178	func cachedRemotesInConfigOrder(ctx context.Context, read func(context.Context) ([]string, error)) []string {
   179		c := cacheFromContext(ctx)
   180		if c == nil {
   181			names, _ := read(ctx) //nolint:errcheck // uncached path keeps the historical best-effort contract
   182			return names
   183		}
   184		snap := c.snapshotFor(ctx)
   185		if snap == nil {
   186			names, _ := read(ctx) //nolint:errcheck // unidentifiable repo: same best-effort contract
   187			return names
   188		}
   189		snap.mu.Lock()
   190		defer snap.mu.Unlock()
   191		if snap.orderedSet {
   192			return snap.ordered
   193		}
   194		names, err := read(ctx)
   195		if err != nil {
   196			// Transient: answer this call, leave the slot unset so the next one retries.
   197			return nil
   198		}
   199		snap.ordered, snap.orderedSet = names, true
   200		return snap.ordered
   201	}
   202	
   203	// cachedIsConfiguredRemote returns the memoized answer for name in this call's
   204	// repository, computing it via probe on a miss. Without a cache installed, or when
   205	// the repository cannot be established, it just calls probe.
   206	//
   207	// A probe that FAILS is never memoized, for the mirror-image reason: a memoized
   208	// false makes ResolveCheckpointSyncRemote fail closed on a configured
   209	// checkpoint_push_remote ("is not a configured git remote") for the rest of the
   210	// process, from one git that could not run.
   211	func cachedIsConfiguredRemote(ctx context.Context, name string, probe func() (bool, error)) bool {
   212		c := cacheFromContext(ctx)
   213		if c == nil {
   214			got, _ := probe() //nolint:errcheck // uncached path keeps the historical best-effort contract
   215			return got
   216		}
   217		snap := c.snapshotFor(ctx)
   218		if snap == nil {
   219			got, _ := probe() //nolint:errcheck // unidentifiable repo: same best-effort contract
   220			return got
   221		}
   222		snap.mu.Lock()
   223		defer snap.mu.Unlock()
   224		if got, ok := snap.member[name]; ok {
   225			return got
   226		}
   227		got, err := probe()
   228		if err != nil {
   229			return false // answer this call; the next one retries
   230		}
   231		snap.member[name] = got
   232		return got
   233	}

1	//go:build integration
     2	
     3	package integration
     4	
     5	import (
     6		"bytes"
     7		"encoding/json"
     8		"errors"
     9		"fmt"
    10		"io/fs"
    11		"os"
    12		"path/filepath"
    13		"strings"
    14		"testing"
    15	
    16		"github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint"
    17		"github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/execx"
    18		"github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/paths"
    19		"github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/testutil"
    20	)
    21	
    22	// =============================================================================
    23	// Single-remote checkpoint sync (ENT-1451)
    24	//
    25	// Checkpoint data syncs to exactly one elected git remote:
    26	// strategy_options.checkpoint_push_remote (fail-closed when the named remote
    27	// is not configured) -> origin -> sole remote -> first
    28	// remote in .git/config order. The branch's tracking config deliberately does
    29	// not participate; see TestCheckpointSyncRemote_BranchTrackingDoesNotReroute.
    30	// The pre-push gate drops checkpoint sync for
    31	// every other remote and for raw-URL pushes, on both backends. The dedicated
    32	// checkpoint_remote URL mode is exempt. These are end-to-end acceptance tests
    33	// through the simulated hook flow; the election precedence itself is
    34	// unit-tested in strategy/checkpoint_sync_remote_test.go.
    35	// =============================================================================
    36	
    37	// remoteTarget names a configured remote and the bare repo backing it.
    38	type remoteTarget struct {
    39		name    string
    40		bareDir string
    41	}
    42	
    43	// queuedCheckpointRefCount returns the git-refs push-discovery queue length
    44	// for the test repo. The queue lives in the git common dir, which for the
    45	// plain (non-worktree) TestEnv repos is .git.
    46	func queuedCheckpointRefCount(t *testing.T, env *TestEnv) int {
    47		t.Helper()
    48		refs, err := checkpoint.NewPushQueue(filepath.Join(env.RepoDir, ".git")).Peek()
    49		if err != nil {
    50			t.Fatalf("read push queue: %v", err)
    51		}
    52		return len(refs)
    53	}
    54	
    55	// assertSingleRemoteRouting drives the pre-push flow first against the
    56	// non-elected remote (no checkpoint data may land there; on git-refs the push
    57	// queue must survive), then against the elected remote (the checkpoint lands
    58	// and the queue drains). Shared by the default-election and config-override
    59	// scenarios, which are mirror images of each other.
    60	//
    61	// expectGatedHint asserts the gated pre-push's output: an automatic election
    62	// must tell the user their checkpoints are waiting for the elected remote and
    63	// name checkpoint_push_remote (the gate was previously a silent no-op —
    64	// checkpoints stranded locally with no signal), while an explicit
    65	// checkpoint_push_remote is a decision already made and must stay quiet.
    66	func assertSingleRemoteRouting(t *testing.T, env *TestEnv, checkpointID string, gated, elected remoteTarget, expectGatedHint bool) {
    67		t.Helper()
    68	
    69		if checkpointID == "" {
    70			t.Fatal("should have a checkpoint ID after condensation")
    71		}
    72		if !env.CheckpointsPresentLocally() {
    73			t.Fatal("checkpoints should exist locally after condensation")
    74		}
    75		if env.usingGitRefs() && queuedCheckpointRefCount(t, env) == 0 {
    76			t.Fatal("git-refs push queue should have entries after condensation")
    77		}
    78	
    79		// Pre-push to the non-elected remote: gated, no checkpoint data escapes.
    80		gatedOutput := env.RunPrePushOutput(gated.name)
    81		if hinted := strings.Contains(gatedOutput, "checkpoint_push_remote"); hinted != expectGatedHint {
    82			t.Errorf("gated pre-push hint presence = %v, want %v; output:\n%s", hinted, expectGatedHint, gatedOutput)
    83		}
    84		if expectGatedHint && !strings.Contains(gatedOutput, fmt.Sprintf("%q", elected.name)) {
    85			t.Errorf("gated pre-push hint should name the elected remote %q; output:\n%s", elected.name, gatedOutput)
    86		}
    87		if env.CheckpointsPresentOnRemote(gated.bareDir) {
    88			t.Errorf("checkpoints should NOT be on non-elected remote %q", gated.name)
    89		}

    10	// CheckpointReadRemotes returns the ordered, deduped remotes that checkpoint
    11	// READS consult: the elected sync remote first, then "origin" as the legacy
    12	// tier (pre-single-remote-sync checkpoints live there, and a fresh clone
    13	// may lack the local settings that elected a non-origin remote).
    14	//
    15	// Unlike the write-side election, this fails OPEN: on an election error
    16	// (misconfigured checkpoint_push_remote, unreadable settings) the chain is
    17	// ["origin"] when configured. Writes fail closed to prevent leaking data;
    18	// failing reads closed would only prevent FINDING data, with no privacy
    19	// benefit. Callers must uphold the read-only rule for every candidate after
    20	// the first: only the elected remote may seed or advance local refs.
    21	//
    22	// An empty result means no candidates — callers needing the "checkpoint
    23	// absent" classification must gather their own positive evidence (successful
    24	// remote listing, readable settings); an empty chain alone is not proof.
    25	//
    26	// The election itself is deliberately un-memoized: every call re-runs it, so a
    27	// settings change or a captured election written mid-invocation is observed
    28	// immediately. What IS memoized, per invocation, are the two .git/config reads
    29	// underneath it — which remotes exist, and does remote X exist (see
    30	// git_remote_cache.go). That split is load-bearing: caching the election result
    31	// would make #1991's capture invisible to the gate that runs right after it.
    32	func CheckpointReadRemotes(ctx context.Context) []string {
    33		return CheckpointReadRemotesWithElection(ctx).Candidates
    34	}

    36	// LeadCheckpointReadRemote returns the head of the read-candidate chain (the
    37	// elected sync remote) for remote.FetchURL's ownership vote. Callers that
    38	// resolve a configured checkpoint_remote pass it as
    39	// FetchURLOptions.LeadReadRemote so the fetch-side inherited check sees the
    40	// same fork-shaped identity the push side sees: in the "cloned the base,
    41	// added a fork" topology only the elected remote's owner exposes the
    42	// mismatch. Returns "" when no candidate resolves.
    43	//
    44	// Pass it only on paths that already confirmed a checkpoint_remote is
    45	// configured. On the no-config path a lead does more than vote: it selects
    46	// which remote serves the fetch.
    47	func LeadCheckpointReadRemote(ctx context.Context) string {
    48		candidates := CheckpointReadRemotes(ctx)
    49		if len(candidates) == 0 {
    50			return ""
    51		}
    52		return candidates[0]
    53	}

    56	// election result it was derived from.

    72	// with the election result it was derived from, so callers that need both —
    73	// e.g. to confine local-ref advancement to the elected remote while iterating
    74	// the chain — make ONE election call instead of two that could disagree if
    75	// settings or remotes change mid-operation. See CheckpointReadRemotes for the
    76	// read-side fail-open rationale and cost note.
    77	func CheckpointReadRemotesWithElection(ctx context.Context) CheckpointReadResolution {

    59	// scenarios, which are mirror images of each other.

    65	// checkpoint_push_remote is a decision already made and must stay quiet.

1	package strategy
     2	
     3	import (
     4		"context"
     5		"fmt"
     6		"log/slog"
     7	
     8		"github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/remote"
     9		"github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/logging"
    10	)
    11	
    12	// refsPushDestination is the single place checkpoint refs are pushed to.
    13	type refsPushDestination struct {
    14		// target is passed to git push and to the recovery fetch: a remote name, or a URL.
    15		target string
    16		// checkpointRemote records that target came from a configured
    17		// checkpoint_remote. It cannot be recovered from target's shape — a
    18		// resolved push URL is URL-shaped too — and it decides both how the
    19		// destination is named and whether the "a checkpoint remote is configured"
    20		// hint applies.
    21		checkpointRemote bool
    22		// ignoredPushURLs counts the push URLs of a multi-URL remote that will NOT
    23		// receive checkpoint refs. Zero in every single-destination topology.
    24		ignoredPushURLs int
    25	}
    26	
    27	// resolveRefsPushDestination picks the single destination for checkpoint-ref
    28	// pushes.
    29	//
    30	// Checkpoint refs need ONE deterministic destination, because the push-discovery
    31	// queue records only a ref (`{"ref": …}`) with no per-destination state: a ref is
    32	// removed from the queue once "the push" succeeds, so "the push" has to mean one
    33	// place. Relying on git's fan-out across a remote's several push URLs breaks that
    34	// in both directions — a single failing URL fails the whole invocation and no ref
    35	// unqueues even though some URLs took it, and an unreachable FIRST URL makes git
    36	// die() before it reaches any later URL at all.
    37	//
    38	// So when a remote carries more than one push URL we target its first push URL
    39	// directly (the one git itself would push to first) and ignore the rest. The
    40	// recovery fetch in fetchAndRebaseRefCommon uses the same target, so — unlike the
    41	// fan-out path, which reconciled the remote's FETCH url while pushing to its
    42	// pushurls — the URL we reconcile is finally the URL we push to.
    43	//
    44	// Consequences, deliberately accepted:
    45	//   - Checkpoint refs live in exactly one repository. Cloning that repository
    46	//     resolves them (its url becomes the clone's fetch URL); cloning a different
    47	//     mirror of the same code does not. Mirroring checkpoints to several
    48	//     repositories is what checkpoint_remote is for.
    49	//   - A first push URL that REJECTS a ref (non-fast-forward) no longer lets later
    50	//     URLs receive it. git would have carried on to them; we stop. That is the
    51	//     price of a deterministic destination, and it is the case the queue can
    52	//     actually reason about.
    53	//
    54	// The git-branch backend deliberately keeps git's fan-out: its v1 branch is a
    55	// single shared ref with no queue to keep coherent, and mirroring it to every
    56	// push URL is behavior users configure their remotes for.
    57	//
    58	// A single push URL keeps the remote NAME as the target rather than resolving it
    59	// to a URL, so the overwhelmingly common topology behaves exactly as before —
    60	// remote-tracking refs still update, output still says "origin", and no
    61	// URL-keyed promisor config appears.
    62	//
    63	// Call this only once there is something to push: it spawns `git remote get-url`
    64	// and its result is unused on an empty queue.
    65	func resolveRefsPushDestination(ctx context.Context, ps pushSettings) refsPushDestination {
    66		target := ps.pushTarget()
    67	
    68		// A configured checkpoint_remote, or a push straight to a URL (git hands the
    69		// hook a bare URL verbatim), is already a single explicit destination.
    70		if ps.hasCheckpointURL() || remote.IsURL(target) {
    71			return refsPushDestination{target: target, checkpointRemote: ps.hasCheckpointURL()}
    72		}
    73	
    74		urls, err := remote.GetPushURLs(ctx, target)
    75		if err != nil {
    76			// Not a configured remote, or git could not report its URLs. Keep the
    77			// target as given; the push itself will report any real problem.
    78			logging.Debug(ctx, "git-refs push: could not enumerate push URLs; using target as given",
    79				slog.String("target", target),
    80				slog.String("error", err.Error()),
    81			)
    82		}
    83		if len(urls) < 2 {
    84			return refsPushDestination{target: target}
    85		}
    86		return refsPushDestination{target: urls[0], ignoredPushURLs: len(urls) - 1}
    87	}
    88	
    89	// display names the destination for progress and warning output.
    90	//
    91	// Deliberately not displayPushTarget: that maps ANY URL to the literal words
    92	// "checkpoint remote", which was only ever true because a URL target implied a
    93	// configured checkpoint_remote. A push URL we resolved ourselves is URL-shaped
    94	// but is not a checkpoint remote, so it is named by its (redacted) URL.
    95	func (d refsPushDestination) display() string {
    96		switch {
    97		case d.checkpointRemote:
    98			return "checkpoint remote"
    99		case d.ignoredPushURLs > 0:
   100			return fmt.Sprintf("%s (first of %d push URLs)", remote.RedactURLOrPath(d.target), d.ignoredPushURLs+1)
   101		default:
   102			return remote.RedactURLOrPath(d.target)
   103		}
   104	}
   105	
   106	// warnIgnoredPushURLs tells the user that checkpoint refs are going to one URL of
   107	// a multi-URL remote — otherwise the choice is invisible and looks like the other
   108	// mirrors silently lost their checkpoints. Call it only when there are refs to
   109	// push, so a no-op push stays quiet.
   110	func (d refsPushDestination) warnIgnoredPushURLs(ctx context.Context) {
   111		if d.ignoredPushURLs == 0 {
   112			return
   113		}
   114		fmt.Fprintf(stderrWriter, "[entire] Checkpoints go to one repository: %s. %d other push URL(s) of this remote will not receive them.\n",
   115			d.display(), d.ignoredPushURLs)
   116		fmt.Fprintln(stderrWriter, "[entire] To store checkpoints in a specific repository instead, set checkpoint_remote in .entire/settings.json.")
   117		logging.Info(ctx, "git-refs push: multi-URL remote, pushing checkpoint refs to the first push URL only",
   118			slog.String("target", remote.RedactURLOrPath(d.target)),
   119			slog.Int("ignored_push_urls", d.ignoredPushURLs),
   120		)
   121	}

---
name: correctness-review
description: Correctness pass over a change -- who owns the write, what survives an interruption, whether the test observes the real contract, and whether the output claims more than the code proves. Use when the user asks for a correctness review, asks whether a change is actually correct or safe to land, or is about to request review on work touching lifecycle, persistence, path resolution, locking, or an external tool's files.
user-invocable: true
disable-model-invocation: false
---

# Correctness Review

**A change is correct when you can name who owns the write, what happens if the process stops on
either side of it, and which test fails on the old code through the real seam.** A diff that reads
well and passes CI has cleared neither bar.

Distilled from the August 2026 Entire CLI review corpus -- nine authored PRs, 40 initial human
inline findings across 244 reviewed PRs. Almost none of the expensive findings were syntax. They
were ownership, state classification, duplicated policy, and tests that watched a nearby
abstraction instead of the failure.

## Use When

- Before requesting review on your own change, or reviewing someone else's diff for correctness
  rather than style.
- The change touches lifecycle, sessions, checkpoints, persistence, hooks, auth, path resolution,
  locking, subprocesses, or files another tool owns.
- Not for abstraction quality and file growth -- that is `thermo-nuclear-code-quality-review`.
  Not for cost -- that is `perf-review`. Not for what breaks outside the diff -- that is
  `blast-radius`. This lens is about whether the change is *true*.

## The three questions

1. **Who owns the write?**
2. **What happens if the process stops immediately before or after the write?**
3. **Which test observes the real contract breaking on the old code?**

If any answer is vague, the change is not ready for review. Answer these first. Everything below
is how to get crisp answers.

## Do

1. **Map the state machine before judging a transition.** For lifecycle, checkpoint, hook, auth,
   or layout work, write the one-page model first: read owner, write owner, migration owner,
   recovery owner; durable state versus temporary state; the operation that makes it irreversible;
   the retry owner after each interruption point; the caller's time budget and every blocking call
   inside it; the user-visible state for success, partial success, and failure. Patching one
   transition without the table is the single most expensive mistake in the corpus.

2. **Trace failures to the outermost outcome.** Follow each new error, timeout, cancellation, and
   skipped operation through every caller to the command, hook, request, or job that the user
   observes. When the Entire Graph plugin is installed (`entire graph version` succeeds),
   enumerate that caller chain with `entire graph impact --repo . --symbol X --format text`
   (direct + transitive callers in one call) and verify against source — the graph can miss
   dynamic dispatch, so it bounds the trace rather than settling it. A safe helper can still be wrong when its error aborts an unrelated workflow. Do not
   approve an internal error policy until you can name the terminal exit status and user-visible
   result it produces.

3. **Audit interruption while resources are held.** For every state that owns a lock, transaction,
   pipe, temporary file, goroutine, or child process, cancel there and identify the cleanup path.
   Process exit is not proof that the domain operation succeeded. After failure, perform the next
   real operation that would expose leaked state; an error assertion alone does not prove cleanup.

4. **Separate safety, liveness, and fairness.** Prove independently that the change cannot corrupt
   state, can eventually make progress, and does not let one caller repeatedly jump queued callers.
   When a shared lock, retry, context, subprocess, or environment helper changes, compare callers
   with a deadline, cancellation without a deadline, and neither. A local fix that changes shared
   blocking or scheduling semantics has a wider contract than its motivating caller.

5. **Separate discovery from mutation authority.** Answer these apart, out loud: which file does
   the external tool read; which file may this command *inspect*; which file may this command
   *mutate*; who owns migration between them; what the user sees when those answers differ.
   Finding a path never grants permission to write to it.

6. **Classify states positively.** `absent` means the OS returned not-exist -- nothing else does.
   `unreadable`, `invalid`, `outdated`, `unresolved`, and `unsupported` are separate states with
   separate remedies. Unknown is not absent. Skipped is not success.

7. **Find the one owner of each decision.** If two functions answer the same eligibility question,
   make them call one predicate. Short duplicated policy is more dangerous than long duplicated
   formatting: one condition drifts and ownership or recovery silently changes. Search by
   responsibility and invariant, not by the symbol name you were about to add.

8. **Push the fix to the deepest boundary that can enforce the invariant once for all callers.**
   Normalize where data becomes permanent rather than pretending the current writer is the only
   producer. Preserve the wire format while you do it.

9. **Prove the test is real.** It fails on the old code for the reported reason, enters through the
   production seam that owns the behavior, and asserts the durable artifact or external result --
   not an intermediate value. Add a negative control. Cover every backend that owns the same
   contract. Use the real `git`, the real protocol, the real lock when that is the source of truth.

10. **Trace every claim to the branch that makes it true.** Comments, status text, warnings,
   remedies, and the PR body are part of the contract. If a message says "removed", a mutation
   happened. If a remedy says "run X", X can fix this exact state. Name the actual recovery owner.

11. **Walk the edge-case matrix** in `references/edge-case-matrix.md` for the categories the change
   touches. These are ordinary Git, filesystem, process, and terminal states, not exotic ones.

12. **Treat every automated finding as a hypothesis.** Reproduce it, check the module's language and
   tool versions, and reply with the mechanism. Do not change correct code to satisfy a linter bot
   working from an outdated model of the language.

13. **Re-scope the moment review changes the ownership model.** Stop patching the old shape. Split
    discovery, mutation, migration, diagnostics, and integration into separate changes whose
    ownership decisions can be reviewed independently.

## Findings

`references/failure-patterns.md` has the seven recurring shapes with worked examples. Scan for them
by name; each one is a finding when present:

- a transition patched without its state machine;
- write ownership inferred from path proximity;
- an error collapsed into absence, or a skip reported as success;
- the same decision ladder in two places;
- a test on a nearby abstraction instead of the production failure;
- output, a comment, or a PR claim the code does not guarantee;
- one diff carrying discovery, mutation, migration, and diagnostics before the contract settled.

## Output

- **The system model**, in a few lines: read owner, write owner, durable write, interruption
  behavior, recovery owner, and outermost user-visible outcome. Say plainly when the change does
  not touch one.
- **Findings**, each with a `file:line`, the pattern it matches, and the state or interruption that
  makes it wrong -- concrete inputs to a wrong result, not a category name.
- **The three questions, answered.** Vague answers are themselves the top finding.
- **Cleanup proof.** Name the real operation performed after failure to prove no residual state
  survives, or mark that property unproven.
- **Cleared.** Which matrix rows you checked and found handled.

# Correctness Review

**A change is correct when you can name who owns the write, what happens if the process stops on
either side of it, and which test fails on the old code through the real seam.** A diff that reads
well and passes CI has cleared neither bar.

inline findings across 244 reviewed PRs. Almost none of the expensive findings were syntax. They
were ownership, state classification, duplicated policy, and tests that watched a nearby
abstraction instead of the failure.

## Use When

- Before requesting review on your own change, or reviewing someone else's diff for correctness
  rather than style.
- The change touches lifecycle, sessions, checkpoints, persistence, hooks, auth, path resolution,
  locking, subprocesses, or files another tool owns.
- Not for abstraction quality and file growth -- that is `thermo-nuclear-code-quality-review`.
  Not for cost -- that is `perf-review`. Not for what breaks outside the diff -- that is
  `blast-radius`. This lens is about whether the change is *true*.

## The three questions

1. **Who owns the write?**
2. **What happens if the process stops immediately before or after the write?**
3. **Which test observes the real contract breaking on the old code?**

If any answer is vague, the change is not ready for review. Answer these first. Everything below
is how to get crisp answers.

1. **Map the state machine before judging a transition.** For lifecycle, checkpoint, hook, auth,
   or layout work, write the one-page model first: read owner, write owner, migration owner,
   recovery owner; durable state versus temporary state; the operation that makes it irreversible;
   the retry owner after each interruption point; the caller's time budget and every blocking call
   inside it; the user-visible state for success, partial success, and failure. Patching one
   transition without the table is the single most expensive mistake in the corpus.

2. **Trace failures to the outermost outcome.** Follow each new error, timeout, cancellation, and
   skipped operation through every caller to the command, hook, request, or job that the user
   observes. When the Entire Graph plugin is installed (`entire graph version` succeeds),
   enumerate that caller chain with `entire graph impact --repo . --symbol X --format text`
   (direct + transitive callers in one call) and verify against source — the graph can miss
   dynamic dispatch, so it bounds the trace rather than settling it. A safe helper can still be wrong when its error aborts an unrelated workflow. Do not
   approve an internal error policy until you can name the terminal exit status and user-visible
   result it produces.

3. **Audit interruption while resources are held.** For every state that owns a lock, transaction,
   pipe, temporary file, goroutine, or child process, cancel there and identify the cleanup path.
   Process exit is not proof that the domain operation succeeded. After failure, perform the next
   real operation that would expose leaked state; an error assertion alone does not prove cleanup.

   state, can eventually make progress, and does not let one caller repeatedly jump queued callers.
   When a shared lock, retry, context, subprocess, or environment helper changes, compare callers
   with a deadline, cancellation without a deadline, and neither. A local fix that changes shared
   blocking or scheduling semantics has a wider contract than its motivating caller.

   the external tool read; which file may this command *inspect*; which file may this command
   *mutate*; who owns migration between them; what the user sees when those answers differ.

# Perf Review

Review a diff for performance regressions. **Tie every claim to a measurement.** Reading source
and asserting something is slow is a hypothesis, not a finding -- if you cannot measure it, say so
and mark the claim unproven rather than reporting it as a regression.

## Use When

- The user asks for a performance review, or whether a diff makes something slower.
- A change touches a hot path, a query, a loop over user-controlled input, or a render path.
- Not for chasing an existing slowness with no diff -- that is `diagnose`, which owns the
  reproduce-and-trace loop.

## Do

1. **Find the cost, don't guess it.** Identify what this diff makes the machine do that it did not
   do before: more queries, more allocations, more round trips, more work per frame. Name the unit.
   Whether changed code sits on a hot path is a caller question — when the Entire Graph plugin is
   installed (`entire graph version` succeeds), answer it with
   `entire graph impact --repo . --symbol X --format text` (direct + transitive callers in one
   call) instead of grepping.
2. **Measure, or mark it unproven.** Run the thing. A benchmark, a query log, a trace, a timed
   script -- whatever is cheap. A number before and a number after. If you cannot get one, say
   "unproven" next to the claim; do not round a suspicion up to a regression.
3. **Check the review-time smells** below. These are the regressions a diff actually introduces,
   as distinct from a system that was always slow.
4. **For each real finding, name the strategy** from the families below that removes the cost.
   A finding without a remedy is a complaint.
5. **Report what you cleared too.** "I checked the N+1 path and it batches correctly" is a finding.

## Review-time smells

The costs a diff adds, in rough order of how often they matter:

- **A query inside a loop.** N+1, whether that is SQL, an HTTP call, or a file read.
- **Work moved onto a hot path.** Serialization, sorting, regex compilation, or logging inside a
  request handler, render, or frame.
- **An unbounded collection.** A loop, fetch, or allocation sized by user input with no limit.
- **A lost index.** A new predicate, join, or sort with nothing backing it.
- **Sync work on an async path.** Blocking I/O, a synchronous read, a lock held across an await.
- **Repeated identical work.** The same computation or fetch on the same inputs within one request.
- **Eager work on a boot or interactive path** that nothing needs yet.

## Strategy families

Hypothesis generators, not a checklist. A family earns an attempt only when the evidence shows the
signal it names; a focused fix for the dominant cost beats applying all eight.

- **Elimination.** The cheapest work is work that doesn't run. Ask whether it needs to exist at
  all -- a computation nobody consumes, a gate always off, a redundant sync. Measurement shows what
  is slow, never that it is deletable, so this one comes from reading, not profiling. When it
  applies, it beats every other family.
- **Divide and conquer.** Cost scales with input size. Chunk, shard, prune, or parallelize.
- **Caching.** The same computation repeats on identical inputs. Store and reuse -- and name what
  invalidates it before claiming the win.
- **Indirection.** An index instead of a scan, a queue that moves work off the interactive path.
  Add the hop only when it removes more from the critical path than it adds.
- **Batching.** Many small operations each paying fixed overhead (RPC, query, syscall). Coalesce.
- **Redundancy.** The wait hangs on one slow attempt: hedge or replicate and take the fastest.
  Trades load for tail latency, so only when the evidence shows the wait dominates.
- **Lazy evaluation.** Cost lands on results never used, or not needed yet. Defer to first use.
- **Scheduling.** The work must happen, but not now. Move it to idle, a background warmup, or
  after the frame commits. The win is perceived latency, so measure the interactive path.

## Output

- **What this diff makes the machine do differently.** The added cost, in a named unit.
- **Findings.** Each with a `file:line`, the smell it matches, a measurement or the word
  `unproven`, and the strategy family that removes it.
- **Cleared.** What you checked and found fine.

## Stop When

Every finding carries either a measurement or an explicit `unproven`, and every real one names a
remedy. A performance review with no numbers anywhere in it has not reviewed performance.

---
name: draft-github-reply
user-invocable: true
disable-model-invocation: false
description: Draft-only safety workflow for GitHub PR, issue, review, and comment replies. Use whenever the user asks to discuss, answer, respond to, comment on, post a reply to, or draft text for a GitHub PR, issue, review, discussion, or comment. The initial request always produces a draft and never publishes; posting is allowed only after the user separately approves the exact draft.
---

# Draft GitHub Reply

Prepare paste-ready GitHub text without publishing it. A comment, review, issue,
or PR update is an external communication made in the user's name, so drafting
and publishing are separate decisions.

## Non-Negotiable Contract

1. Treat every initial request involving a GitHub reply or comment as
   **draft-only**, including wording such as "comment on this issue," "post my
   reply," "respond there," or "reply to the maintainer."
2. Do not call any write-capable GitHub command or API while drafting. This
   includes `gh issue comment`, `gh pr comment`, `gh pr review`, `gh api` with a
   mutating method, GraphQL mutations, or equivalent browser actions.
3. Read-only inspection is allowed when useful: inspect the issue, PR, linked
   comment, reviews, and local code to understand context.
4. Return only the proposed reply unless the user also asks for analysis. Do
   not preface it with a plan or discussion of what the reply will say.
5. After presenting the draft, wait. Do not publish it in the same turn.
6. Publish only when a later user message explicitly approves that exact draft
   and explicitly instructs publication, for example:
   - "Post that exact draft."
   - "Approved, publish it on issue #123."
   - "Use the second version and post it."
7. Treat revisions as a new draft. If the user changes wording, present the
   revised text and wait for fresh explicit approval before publishing.
8. Approval to publish one draft applies only to the named destination and
   exact text. Do not reuse it for another PR, issue, review, or comment.
9. If approval or the destination is ambiguous, ask one short clarifying
   question instead of publishing.

## Output

When only a draft is requested, output the paste-ready text with no quotation
marks and no extra explanation. If context or assumptions materially affect the
wording, put a short note after the draft, not before it.

When the user explicitly asks to understand a maintainer's point as well as
draft a response, use:

**Draft**

[paste-ready reply]

**Interpretation**

[concise explanation]

The interpretation is for the user and must not be included in a later posted
comment unless the user explicitly approves it as part of the draft.

## Examples

Initial request: "Comment on this issue and explain what the maintainer means."

Action: inspect read-only context, provide a draft and interpretation, and do
not post.

Initial request: "Post a reply saying the fix is ready."

Action: draft the reply only. The word "post" in the initial request does not
authorize publication.

Follow-up: "That looks good."

Action: do not post because this approves quality but does not explicitly
instruct publication. Wait or ask whether the user wants it published.

Follow-up: "Post that exact draft on PR #42."

Action: publication is authorized for that exact draft on PR #42 only.

# Draft GitHub Reply

Prepare paste-ready GitHub text without publishing it. A comment, review, issue,
or PR update is an external communication made in the user's name, so drafting
and publishing are separate decisions.

## Non-Negotiable Contract

1. Treat every initial request involving a GitHub reply or comment as
   **draft-only**, including wording such as "comment on this issue," "post my
   reply," "respond there," or "reply to the maintainer."
2. Do not call any write-capable GitHub command or API while drafting. This
   includes `gh issue comment`, `gh pr comment`, `gh pr review`, `gh api` with a
   mutating method, GraphQL mutations, or equivalent browser actions.
3. Read-only inspection is allowed when useful: inspect the issue, PR, linked
   comment, reviews, and local code to understand context.
4. Return only the proposed reply unless the user also asks for analysis. Do
   not preface it with a plan or discussion of what the reply will say.
5. After presenting the draft, wait. Do not publish it in the same turn.
6. Publish only when a later user message explicitly approves that exact draft
   and explicitly instructs publication, for example:
   - "Post that exact draft."
   - "Approved, publish it on issue #123."
   - "Use the second version and post it."

   revised text and wait for fresh explicit approval before publishing.

   exact text. Do not reuse it for another PR, issue, review, or comment.
9. If approval or the destination is ambiguous, ask one short clarifying
   question instead of publishing.

When only a draft is requested, output the paste-ready text with no quotation
marks and no extra explanation. If context or assumptions materially affect the

# Blast Radius

Find what a change breaks somewhere else, before it ships.

Companion to `research-codebase` and `explain`. `research-codebase` tells you what the code does.
`explain` tells you why it's shaped that way. Blast radius tells you what it breaks somewhere else.

Listing the callers is not the job. You can grep those in a second. The job is the breakage grep
won't show you.

## Use When

- The user asks for the blast radius of a change, or what it could break.
- You are reviewing a small diff you don't trust yet.
- A change touches a shared path, a wire format, or a dependency you don't own.

## Don't Trust Your Own Writeup

A blast-radius writeup that sounds right is worthless. It reads as convincing whether or not it's
true, and that is the trap. Don't hand back the writeup. Find the one or two facts the whole thing
depends on and prove them by running code. Words are where you start, not what you ship.

### How Sure Are You

For each fact the change's safety depends on, get it as far down this list as is cheap, and say
where it stopped.

1. You said so. Worthless on its own.
2. You pointed at the line. A real `file:line`, or the library's own source.
3. You showed the bad case can't happen. You walked the failure step by step and it doesn't reach.
4. You ran it. A script or test that calls the real code and fails loud if you're wrong.
5. You reproduced it in the running app.

Any safety fact you can't get to step 4, say so out loud. Don't write it up as settled. Step 4 is
usually one small script that imports the same library the app ships and calls the exact function
you're worried about.

## Do

1. **Read the change.** The diff, the symbols it adds, changes, and deletes, and what it now does
   differently, including the part the diff doesn't spell out. Pull the surrounding history with
   `git log -p $(git merge-base main HEAD)..HEAD` and `gh pr view` when a PR exists.
1b. **Sweep the mechanical radius with the graph when installed** (`entire graph version`
   succeeds). One call per changed symbol replaces the caller grep and adds what grep misses
   structurally — type consumers, data flows, co-change files:
   `entire graph impact --repo . --symbol X --format text`. For a branch-wide change list,
   `entire graph diff --base <base> --head HEAD --json`. Graph output is evidence, not an
   oracle — it can miss callers (dynamic dispatch, interfaces), so it bounds step 3, never
   replaces it.
2. **Find the one fact it's safe because of.** Most changes that look scary are safe because of a
   single fact, like "this call only drops already-dead cache entries and does nothing else". Find
   that fact. If it holds, most of the scary cases die at once. Spend your time here, not on a long
   list of maybes.
3. **Look where grep stops.** Read the source of the library you call, and check its pinned version
   and any local patch. Work out when things run: microtasks, unmount and teardown, framework
   scheduling differences. Follow what a symbol search misses: the JSON an API returns, a DB column,
   a wire format, another language reading the same bytes, a feature flag, code three hops downstream.
4. **Audit semantic callers of shared primitives.** When a lock, retry, context, subprocess, or
   environment helper changes, compare callers with a deadline, cancellation without a deadline,
   and neither. Trace blocking, fairness, error identity, cleanup, inherited environment, and the
   outermost workflow result. Symbol callers are not enough when the changed contract is scheduling
   or process behavior.
5. **Be honest about each risk.** Give it a real chance of happening and a real cost if it does.
   Keep the risks you confirmed; list the ones you checked and cleared separately. Cite a real
   `file:line`. A search that finds nothing is still an answer. Never make up a caller or an API.
6. **Prove the one fact.** Write a script or test that runs the real code, run it, and paste what
   happened. If you can't prove it cheaply, mark it unproven. Don't round up.
7. **For a big or wide change, run it as an `arena`.** Ask several models the same question and merge
   the answers. Different models catch different real bugs.

## Output

- **What it does.** What changed, including the part that isn't obvious.
- **The one fact it's safe because of.** State it, say which step you got it to, and show the proof.
  If you couldn't prove it, write unproven.
- **Risks.** Only the real ones. Each names how it breaks, the `file:line`, how likely and how bad,
  and how to check. Paste the proof for the ones that matter.
- **Cleared.** What you checked and why it's fine.
- **Before you merge.** The cheapest test or repro that catches the real bug, including the script
  you wrote.

Write it through `unslop`, cite real code, and strip anything private before it goes anywhere public.

## Stop When

The one safety fact is either proven at step 4 or explicitly marked unproven. A writeup that
asserts safety without naming which step its central fact reached means this failed.

# Correctness Review

**A change is correct when you can name who owns the write, what happens if the process stops on
either side of it, and which test fails on the old code through the real seam.** A diff that reads
well and passes CI has cleared neither bar.

Distilled from the August 2026 Entire CLI review corpus -- nine authored PRs, 40 initial human
inline findings across 244 reviewed PRs. Almost none of the expensive findings were syntax. They
were ownership, state classification, duplicated policy, and tests that watched a nearby
abstraction instead of the failure.

## Use When

- Before requesting review on your own change, or reviewing someone else's diff for correctness
  rather than style.
- The change touches lifecycle, sessions, checkpoints, persistence, hooks, auth, path resolution,
  locking, subprocesses, or files another tool owns.
- Not for abstraction quality and file growth -- that is `thermo-nuclear-code-quality-review`.
  Not for cost -- that is `perf-review`. Not for what breaks outside the diff -- that is
  `blast-radius`. This lens is about whether the change is *true*.

## The three questions

1. **Who owns the write?**
2. **What happens if the process stops immediately before or after the write?**
3. **Which test observes the real contract breaking on the old code?**

If any answer is vague, the change is not ready for review. Answer these first. Everything below
is how to get crisp answers.

## Do

1. **Map the state machine before judging a transition.** For lifecycle, checkpoint, hook, auth,
   or layout work, write the one-page model first: read owner, write owner, migration owner,
   recovery owner; durable state versus temporary state; the operation that makes it irreversible;
   the retry owner after each interruption point; the caller's time budget and every blocking call
   inside it; the user-visible state for success, partial success, and failure. Patching one
   transition without the table is the single most expensive mistake in the corpus.

2. **Trace failures to the outermost outcome.** Follow each new error, timeout, cancellation, and
   skipped operation through every caller to the command, hook, request, or job that the user
   observes. When the Entire Graph plugin is installed (`entire graph version` succeeds),
   enumerate that caller chain with `entire graph impact --repo . --symbol X --format text`
   (direct + transitive callers in one call) and verify against source — the graph can miss
   dynamic dispatch, so it bounds the trace rather than settling it. A safe helper can still be wrong when its error aborts an unrelated workflow. Do not
   approve an internal error policy until you can name the terminal exit status and user-visible
   result it produces.

3. **Audit interruption while resources are held.** For every state that owns a lock, transaction,
   pipe, temporary file, goroutine, or child process, cancel there and identify the cleanup path.
   Process exit is not proof that the domain operation succeeded. After failure, perform the next
   real operation that would expose leaked state; an error assertion alone does not prove cleanup.

4. **Separate safety, liveness, and fairness.** Prove independently that the change cannot corrupt
   state, can eventually make progress, and does not let one caller repeatedly jump queued callers.
   When a shared lock, retry, context, subprocess, or environment helper changes, compare callers
   with a deadline, cancellation without a deadline, and neither. A local fix that changes shared
   blocking or scheduling semantics has a wider contract than its motivating caller.

5. **Separate discovery from mutation authority.** Answer these apart, out loud: which file does
   the external tool read; which file may this command *inspect*; which file may this command
   *mutate*; who owns migration between them; what the user sees when those answers differ.
   Finding a path never grants permission to write to it.

6. **Classify states positively.** `absent` means the OS returned not-exist -- nothing else does.
   `unreadable`, `invalid`, `outdated`, `unresolved`, and `unsupported` are separate states with
   separate remedies. Unknown is not absent. Skipped is not success.

7. **Find the one owner of each decision.** If two functions answer the same eligibility question,
   make them call one predicate. Short duplicated policy is more dangerous than long duplicated
   formatting: one condition drifts and ownership or recovery silently changes. Search by
   responsibility and invariant, not by the symbol name you were about to add.

8. **Push the fix to the deepest boundary that can enforce the invariant once for all callers.**
   Normalize where data becomes permanent rather than pretending the current writer is the only
   producer. Preserve the wire format while you do it.

9. **Prove the test is real.** It fails on the old code for the reported reason, enters through the
   production seam that owns the behavior, and asserts the durable artifact or external result --
   not an intermediate value. Add a negative control. Cover every backend that owns the same
   contract. Use the real `git`, the real protocol, the real lock when that is the source of truth.

10. **Trace every claim to the branch that makes it true.** Comments, status text, warnings,
   remedies, and the PR body are part of the contract. If a message says "removed", a mutation
   happened. If a remedy says "run X", X can fix this exact state. Name the actual recovery owner.

11. **Walk the edge-case matrix** in `references/edge-case-matrix.md` for the categories the change
   touches. These are ordinary Git, filesystem, process, and terminal states, not exotic ones.

12. **Treat every automated finding as a hypothesis.** Reproduce it, check the module's language and
   tool versions, and reply with the mechanism. Do not change correct code to satisfy a linter bot
   working from an outdated model of the language.

13. **Re-scope the moment review changes the ownership model.** Stop patching the old shape. Split
    discovery, mutation, migration, diagnostics, and integration into separate changes whose
    ownership decisions can be reviewed independently.

## Findings

`references/failure-patterns.md` has the seven recurring shapes with worked examples. Scan for them
by name; each one is a finding when present:

- a transition patched without its state machine;
- write ownership inferred from path proximity;
- an error collapsed into absence, or a skip reported as success;
- the same decision ladder in two places;
- a test on a nearby abstraction instead of the production failure;
- output, a comment, or a PR claim the code does not guarantee;
- one diff carrying discovery, mutation, migration, and diagnostics before the contract settled.

## Output

- **The system model**, in a few lines: read owner, write owner, durable write, interruption
  behavior, recovery owner, and outermost user-visible outcome. Say plainly when the change does
  not touch one.
- **Findings**, each with a `file:line`, the pattern it matches, and the state or interruption that
  makes it wrong -- concrete inputs to a wrong result, not a category name.
- **The three questions, answered.** Vague answers are themselves the top finding.
- **Cleanup proof.** Name the real operation performed after failure to prove no residual state
  survives, or mark that property unproven.
- **Cleared.** Which matrix rows you checked and found handled.

# Perf Review

Review a diff for performance regressions. **Tie every claim to a measurement.** Reading source
and asserting something is slow is a hypothesis, not a finding -- if you cannot measure it, say so
and mark the claim unproven rather than reporting it as a regression.

## Use When

- The user asks for a performance review, or whether a diff makes something slower.
- A change touches a hot path, a query, a loop over user-controlled input, or a render path.
- Not for chasing an existing slowness with no diff -- that is `diagnose`, which owns the
  reproduce-and-trace loop.

## Do

1. **Find the cost, don't guess it.** Identify what this diff makes the machine do that it did not
   do before: more queries, more allocations, more round trips, more work per frame. Name the unit.
   Whether changed code sits on a hot path is a caller question — when the Entire Graph plugin is
   installed (`entire graph version` succeeds), answer it with
   `entire graph impact --repo . --symbol X --format text` (direct + transitive callers in one
   call) instead of grepping.
2. **Measure, or mark it unproven.** Run the thing. A benchmark, a query log, a trace, a timed
   script -- whatever is cheap. A number before and a number after. If you cannot get one, say
   "unproven" next to the claim; do not round a suspicion up to a regression.
3. **Check the review-time smells** below. These are the regressions a diff actually introduces,
   as distinct from a system that was always slow.
4. **For each real finding, name the strategy** from the families below that removes the cost.
   A finding without a remedy is a complaint.
5. **Report what you cleared too.** "I checked the N+1 path and it batches correctly" is a finding.

## Review-time smells

The costs a diff adds, in rough order of how often they matter:

- **A query inside a loop.** N+1, whether that is SQL, an HTTP call, or a file read.
- **Work moved onto a hot path.** Serialization, sorting, regex compilation, or logging inside a
  request handler, render, or frame.
- **An unbounded collection.** A loop, fetch, or allocation sized by user input with no limit.
- **A lost index.** A new predicate, join, or sort with nothing backing it.
- **Sync work on an async path.** Blocking I/O, a synchronous read, a lock held across an await.
- **Repeated identical work.** The same computation or fetch on the same inputs within one request.
- **Eager work on a boot or interactive path** that nothing needs yet.

## Strategy families

Hypothesis generators, not a checklist. A family earns an attempt only when the evidence shows the
signal it names; a focused fix for the dominant cost beats applying all eight.

- **Elimination.** The cheapest work is work that doesn't run. Ask whether it needs to exist at
  all -- a computation nobody consumes, a gate always off, a redundant sync. Measurement shows what
  is slow, never that it is deletable, so this one comes from reading, not profiling. When it
  applies, it beats every other family.
- **Divide and conquer.** Cost scales with input size. Chunk, shard, prune, or parallelize.
- **Caching.** The same computation repeats on identical inputs. Store and reuse -- and name what
  invalidates it before claiming the win.
- **Indirection.** An index instead of a scan, a queue that moves work off the interactive path.
  Add the hop only when it removes more from the critical path than it adds.
- **Batching.** Many small operations each paying fixed overhead (RPC, query, syscall). Coalesce.
- **Redundancy.** The wait hangs on one slow attempt: hedge or replicate and take the fastest.
  Trades load for tail latency, so only when the evidence shows the wait dominates.
- **Lazy evaluation.** Cost lands on results never used, or not needed yet. Defer to first use.
- **Scheduling.** The work must happen, but not now. Move it to idle, a background warmup, or
  after the frame commits. The win is perceived latency, so measure the interactive path.

## Output

- **What this diff makes the machine do differently.** The added cost, in a named unit.
- **Findings.** Each with a `file:line`, the smell it matches, a measurement or the word
  `unproven`, and the strategy family that removes it.
- **Cleared.** What you checked and found fine.

## Stop When

Every finding carries either a measurement or an explicit `unproven`, and every real one names a
remedy. A performance review with no numbers anywhere in it has not reviewed performance.

(exit 0)

# Blast Radius

Find what a change breaks somewhere else, before it ships.

Companion to `research-codebase` and `explain`. `research-codebase` tells you what the code does.
`explain` tells you why it's shaped that way. Blast radius tells you what it breaks somewhere else.

Listing the callers is not the job. You can grep those in a second. The job is the breakage grep
won't show you.

## Use When

- The user asks for the blast radius of a change, or what it could break.
- You are reviewing a small diff you don't trust yet.
- A change touches a shared path, a wire format, or a dependency you don't own.

## Don't Trust Your Own Writeup

A blast-radius writeup that sounds right is worthless. It reads as convincing whether or not it's
true, and that is the trap. Don't hand back the writeup. Find the one or two facts the whole thing
depends on and prove them by running code. Words are where you start, not what you ship.

### How Sure Are You

For each fact the change's safety depends on, get it as far down this list as is cheap, and say
where it stopped.

1. You said so. Worthless on its own.
2. You pointed at the line. A real `file:line`, or the library's own source.
3. You showed the bad case can't happen. You walked the failure step by step and it doesn't reach.
4. You ran it. A script or test that calls the real code and fails loud if you're wrong.
5. You reproduced it in the running app.

Any safety fact you can't get to step 4, say so out loud. Don't write it up as settled. Step 4 is
usually one small script that imports the same library the app ships and calls the exact function
you're worried about.

## Do

1. **Read the change.** The diff, the symbols it adds, changes, and deletes, and what it now does
   differently, including the part the diff doesn't spell out. Pull the surrounding history with
   `git log -p $(git merge-base main HEAD)..HEAD` and `gh pr view` when a PR exists.
1b. **Sweep the mechanical radius with the graph when installed** (`entire graph version`
   succeeds). One call per changed symbol replaces the caller grep and adds what grep misses
   structurally — type consumers, data flows, co-change files:
   `entire graph impact --repo . --symbol X --format text`. For a branch-wide change list,
   `entire graph diff --base <base> --head HEAD --json`. Graph output is evidence, not an
   oracle — it can miss callers (dynamic dispatch, interfaces), so it bounds step 3, never
   replaces it.
2. **Find the one fact it's safe because of.** Most changes that look scary are safe because of a
   single fact, like "this call only drops already-dead cache entries and does nothing else". Find
   that fact. If it holds, most of the scary cases die at once. Spend your time here, not on a long
   list of maybes.
3. **Look where grep stops.** Read the source of the library you call, and check its pinned version
   and any local patch. Work out when things run: microtasks, unmount and teardown, framework
   scheduling differences. Follow what a symbol search misses: the JSON an API returns, a DB column,
   a wire format, another language reading the same bytes, a feature flag, code three hops downstream.
4. **Audit semantic callers of shared primitives.** When a lock, retry, context, subprocess, or
   environment helper changes, compare callers with a deadline, cancellation without a deadline,
   and neither. Trace blocking, fairness, error identity, cleanup, inherited environment, and the
   outermost workflow result. Symbol callers are not enough when the changed contract is scheduling
   or process behavior.
5. **Be honest about each risk.** Give it a real chance of happening and a real cost if it does.
   Keep the risks you confirmed; list the ones you checked and cleared separately. Cite a real
   `file:line`. A search that finds nothing is still an answer. Never make up a caller or an API.
6. **Prove the one fact.** Write a script or test that runs the real code, run it, and paste what
   happened. If you can't prove it cheaply, mark it unproven. Don't round up.
7. **For a big or wide change, run it as an `arena`.** Ask several models the same question and merge
   the answers. Different models catch different real bugs.

## Output

- **What it does.** What changed, including the part that isn't obvious.
- **The one fact it's safe because of.** State it, say which step you got it to, and show the proof.
  If you couldn't prove it, write unproven.
- **Risks.** Only the real ones. Each names how it breaks, the `file:line`, how likely and how bad,
  and how to check. Paste the proof for the ones that matter.
- **Cleared.** What you checked and why it's fine.
- **Before you merge.** The cheapest test or repro that catches the real bug, including the script
  you wrote.

Write it through `unslop`, cite real code, and strip anything private before it goes anywhere public.

## Stop When

The one safety fact is either proven at step 4 or explicitly marked unproven. A writeup that
asserts safety without naming which step its central fact reached means this failed.

(exit 0)

# Draft GitHub Reply

Prepare paste-ready GitHub text without publishing it. A comment, review, issue,
or PR update is an external communication made in the user's name, so drafting
and publishing are separate decisions.

## Non-Negotiable Contract

1. Treat every initial request involving a GitHub reply or comment as
   **draft-only**, including wording such as "comment on this issue," "post my
   reply," "respond there," or "reply to the maintainer."
2. Do not call any write-capable GitHub command or API while drafting. This
   includes `gh issue comment`, `gh pr comment`, `gh pr review`, `gh api` with a
   mutating method, GraphQL mutations, or equivalent browser actions.
3. Read-only inspection is allowed when useful: inspect the issue, PR, linked
   comment, reviews, and local code to understand context.
4. Return only the proposed reply unless the user also asks for analysis. Do
   not preface it with a plan or discussion of what the reply will say.
5. After presenting the draft, wait. Do not publish it in the same turn.
6. Publish only when a later user message explicitly approves that exact draft
   and explicitly instructs publication, for example:
   - "Post that exact draft."
   - "Approved, publish it on issue #123."
   - "Use the second version and post it."
7. Treat revisions as a new draft. If the user changes wording, present the
   revised text and wait for fresh explicit approval before publishing.
8. Approval to publish one draft applies only to the named destination and
   exact text. Do not reuse it for another PR, issue, review, or comment.
9. If approval or the destination is ambiguous, ask one short clarifying
   question instead of publishing.

## Output

When only a draft is requested, output the paste-ready text with no quotation
marks and no extra explanation. If context or assumptions materially affect the
wording, put a short note after the draft, not before it.

When the user explicitly asks to understand a maintainer's point as well as
draft a response, use:

**Draft**

[paste-ready reply]

**Interpretation**

[concise explanation]

The interpretation is for the user and must not be included in a later posted
comment unless the user explicitly approves it as part of the draft.

## Examples

Initial request: "Comment on this issue and explain what the maintainer means."

Action: inspect read-only context, provide a draft and interpretation, and do
not post.

Initial request: "Post a reply saying the fix is ready."

Action: draft the reply only. The word "post" in the initial request does not
authorize publication.

Follow-up: "That looks good."

Action: do not post because this approves quality but does not explicitly
instruct publication. Wait or ask whether the user wants it published.

Follow-up: "Post that exact draft on PR #42."

Action: publication is authorized for that exact draft on PR #42 only.

(exit 0)

- [ ] Absent

- [ ] Current

- [ ] Unresolved

- [ ] Cancellation before the durable write
- [ ] Cancellation during each state that holds an external resource or prepared transaction
- [ ] Cancellation after the write but before state save
- [ ] Graceful abort releases locks, temporary files, pipes, goroutines, and child processes
- [ ] The next real operation succeeds immediately after cancellation or failure
- [ ] Lock contention and lock timeout

- [ ] Shared blocking, polling, or retry changes audited across all caller classes

- [ ] Cleanup that removes state a later step needs
- [ ] Retry after a partial operation
- [ ] Idempotent rerun

## Environment and user interaction

- [ ] Variable unset
- [ ] Variable present but empty
- [ ] Tool-specific inherited variables cannot override the explicitly selected target
- [ ] Ambient variables poisoned in tests to prove repository, config, and credential isolation
- [ ] No TTY
- [ ] Raw-mode TTY
- [ ] `NO_COLOR` or non-styled output
- [ ] Windows and missing POSIX shell
- [ ] Expired, missing, and explicitly selected login contexts

## Failure semantics

- [ ] Typed sentinel errors matched with `errors.Is`, never by string
- [ ] Presence distinguished from a non-empty value (`os.LookupEnv`)
- [ ] Caller cancellation propagated separately from a child timeout
- [ ] Process exit success distinguished from domain-operation success
- [ ] Protocol response, process result, and local cancellation state agree
- [ ] Internal timeout or contention traced to the outermost command, hook, request, or job result
- [ ] Contention or temporary unavailability is not reported as a data conflict
- [ ] Context-aware lock acquisition wherever a context exists
- [ ] The underlying error preserved unless the public contract deliberately replaces it
- [ ] A silent-error type used only when the command already printed the user-facing error
- [ ] Unreadable, malformed, or unresolved never turned into absent
- [ ] No success reported after skipping every requested target

## User-visible contract

- [ ] Every status has a distinct meaning
- [ ] Every success message follows a confirmed success
- [ ] Every warning names the affected path, remote, context, or agent when that helps
- [ ] Every remedy can fix the exact state that printed it
- [ ] The command does not print the same error twice
- [ ] Comments and docs name the actual recovery owner and execution path

## Test hygiene

- [ ] Focused test shown failing on the old code, then passing
- [ ] Entry through the production seam, not a nearby helper
- [ ] Outermost affected workflow result asserted, not only the helper's return value
- [ ] Assertion on the durable artifact or external result
- [ ] Aftermath checked with the next real operation that would expose leaked state
- [ ] Negative control proving unrelated behavior did not change
- [ ] Every backend that owns the same contract covered
- [ ] Native tooling or the real protocol used where it is the source of truth
- [ ] Real lock held, or the real competing operation run, for concurrency claims
- [ ] Related log fields asserted on the same record
- [ ] Raw serialized bytes asserted when encoding shape is part of the contract
- [ ] Parallel by default, except where the test mutates process-global state
- [ ] Isolated temporary repository, config directory, cache, and token storage
- [ ] No spawned binary inherits an interactive terminal

## Language-level choices that encode semantics (Go)

- Keep `ctx` bound to the caller context; name a derived timeout for its purpose
  (`discoveryCtx`), never shadow the caller's.
- Distinguish `os.ErrNotExist` from permission and I/O errors.
- Keep atomic writes, containment validation, and symlink policy together -- atomic replacement
  alone does not define safe ownership.
- Preserve file modes and unknown fields when editing user-owned configuration.
- Create a happens-before edge with a channel, mutex, or atomic in race-tested code.
- Treat `exec.Cmd.Wait` as a process result, not proof that a child protocol committed its operation.
- Inspect `exec.Cmd.Cancel` before using the default kill behavior for a stateful child protocol.
- Record local cancellation state when a cooperative child abort can still exit successfully.
- Close resources at the right lifetime boundary; a cleanup that deletes state is not the same
  operation as terminating a process.
- Check the module's language version before accepting syntax advice.

item.stdout:
# Correctness failure patterns

The seven shapes the strongest review comments kept finding. Each entry: what it looks like, a
worked example from the corpus, and what to do instead.

## 1. A transition patched without its state machine

The idea is right, the adjacent transitions are wrong.

Reserving a checkpoint ID before an interruptible write so recovery reuses the same identity was
correct. What review found around it: reservation and condensation each decided independently
whether a session had content; the new state mutation added a blocking lock inside a three-second
`SessionEnd` budget; a task-only session could have `StepCount == 0` and no shadow branch yet still
hold durable work; a comment named the post-commit path as the retry owner when `doctor` owned
that recovery case.

**Instead:** write the transition table first -- phase, files, transcript content, task records,
durable writes, identity, retry owner, cancellation timing. Two functions answering the same
eligibility question must call one predicate.

## 2. Write ownership inferred from path proximity

An external tool reads its config from the root checkout; the command may be invoked from a linked
worktree. Treating the discovered path as a natural mutation target was unsafe in six distinct
ways: a derived root could resolve to `$HOME`, a tool's home directory, a bare repository's parent,
or somewhere outside the checkout; a directory or file symlink could redirect the write; a scratch
worktree could modify a tracked file belonging to another checkout; an unreadable file could be
reported as successfully removed; repository-wide hooks could stay active while the picker called
the agent absent; a valid root-checkout setup drew the same warning as a broken one.

**Instead:** answer read / inspect / mutate / migrate / explain as five separate questions.
Discovery does not grant mutation authority.

## 3. An error collapsed into absence, or a skip reported as success

narrow and reusing the shared helper; rejecting a wrong review suggestion with evidence.

mutation authority -- into design work before the diff exists.

# Edge-case matrix

Walk the categories the change touches. These are ordinary states, not exotic ones -- every row
below appeared as a real review finding or a real bug.

## Git and paths

- [ ] Normal checkout
- [ ] Conventional linked worktree
- [ ] `.bare/worktrees` layout
- [ ] Separate Git directory
- [ ] Ordinary submodule
- [ ] Linked submodule
- [ ] Symlinked checkout or directory
- [ ] Symlinked final file, and dangling symlink
- [ ] Missing, unreadable, malformed, and non-regular paths
- [ ] Path containment still holds *after* symlink resolution
- [ ] No remote, fork remote, raw URL, multiple push URLs, elected remote

## State and persistence

- [ ] Absent
- [ ] User-owned but not managed by this tool
- [ ] Partial
- [ ] Current
- [ ] Outdated
- [ ] Invalid
- [ ] Unreadable
- [ ] Unresolved
- [ ] Unsupported
- [ ] Older persisted format
- [ ] Unknown fields preserved on rewrite
- [ ] Nil versus empty serialized values (`null` versus `[]`)

## Process and concurrency

- [ ] Cancellation before the durable write
- [ ] Cancellation during each state that holds an external resource or prepared transaction
- [ ] Cancellation after the write but before state save
- [ ] Graceful abort releases locks, temporary files, pipes, goroutines, and child processes
- [ ] The next real operation succeeds immediately after cancellation or failure
- [ ] Lock contention and lock timeout
- [ ] Safety, liveness, and fairness evaluated separately
- [ ] Deadline-bearing, cancelable-without-deadline, and non-cancelable callers retain their contract
- [ ] Shared blocking, polling, or retry changes audited across all caller classes
- [ ] Concurrent writer from another process (the real one, not an in-process stand-in)
- [ ] Cleanup that removes state a later step needs
- [ ] Retry after a partial operation
- [ ] Idempotent rerun

## Environment and user interaction

- [ ] Variable unset
- [ ] Variable present but empty
- [ ] Tool-specific inherited variables cannot override the explicitly selected target
- [ ] Ambient variables poisoned in tests to prove repository, config, and credential isolation
- [ ] No TTY
- [ ] Raw-mode TTY
- [ ] `NO_COLOR` or non-styled output
- [ ] Windows and missing POSIX shell
- [ ] Expired, missing, and explicitly selected login contexts

## Failure semantics

- [ ] Typed sentinel errors matched with `errors.Is`, never by string
- [ ] Presence distinguished from a non-empty value (`os.LookupEnv`)
- [ ] Caller cancellation propagated separately from a child timeout
- [ ] Process exit success distinguished from domain-operation success
- [ ] Protocol response, process result, and local cancellation state agree
- [ ] Internal timeout or contention traced to the outermost command, hook, request, or job result
- [ ] Contention or temporary unavailability is not reported as a data conflict
- [ ] Context-aware lock acquisition wherever a context exists
- [ ] The underlying error preserved unless the public contract deliberately replaces it
- [ ] A silent-error type used only when the command already printed the user-facing error
- [ ] Unreadable, malformed, or unresolved never turned into absent
- [ ] No success reported after skipping every requested target

## User-visible contract

- [ ] Every status has a distinct meaning
- [ ] Every success message follows a confirmed success
- [ ] Every warning names the affected path, remote, context, or agent when that helps
- [ ] Every remedy can fix the exact state that printed it
- [ ] The command does not print the same error twice
- [ ] Comments and docs name the actual recovery owner and execution path

## Test hygiene

- [ ] Focused test shown failing on the old code, then passing
- [ ] Entry through the production seam, not a nearby helper
- [ ] Outermost affected workflow result asserted, not only the helper's return value
- [ ] Assertion on the durable artifact or external result
- [ ] Aftermath checked with the next real operation that would expose leaked state
- [ ] Negative control proving unrelated behavior did not change
- [ ] Every backend that owns the same contract covered
- [ ] Native tooling or the real protocol used where it is the source of truth
- [ ] Real lock held, or the real competing operation run, for concurrency claims
- [ ] Related log fields asserted on the same record
- [ ] Raw serialized bytes asserted when encoding shape is part of the contract
- [ ] Parallel by default, except where the test mutates process-global state
- [ ] Isolated temporary repository, config directory, cache, and token storage
- [ ] No spawned binary inherits an interactive terminal

## Language-level choices that encode semantics (Go)

- Keep `ctx` bound to the caller context; name a derived timeout for its purpose
  (`discoveryCtx`), never shadow the caller's.
- Distinguish `os.ErrNotExist` from permission and I/O errors.
- Keep atomic writes, containment validation, and symlink policy together -- atomic replacement
  alone does not define safe ownership.
- Preserve file modes and unknown fields when editing user-owned configuration.
- Create a happens-before edge with a channel, mutex, or atomic in race-tested code.
- Treat `exec.Cmd.Wait` as a process result, not proof that a child protocol committed its operation.
- Inspect `exec.Cmd.Cancel` before using the default kill behavior for a stateful child protocol.
- Record local cancellation state when a cooperative child abort can still exit successfully.
- Close resources at the right lifetime boundary; a cleanup that deletes state is not the same
  operation as terminating a process.
- Check the module's language version before accepting syntax advice.

   226		assert.Equal(t, 2, probeCalls, "invalidation must clear membership answers too")

   236	// InvalidateGitRemoteCache for exactly this reason.

   240		testutil.IsolateGitConfigEnv(t)
   241		dir := t.TempDir()

   243		testutil.WriteFile(t, dir, "f.txt", "x")
   244		testutil.GitAdd(t, dir, "f.txt")
   245		testutil.GitCommit(t, dir, "init")
   246		t.Chdir(dir)

   249		testutil.AddRemote(t, dir, "origin", "https://example.com/origin.git")

   252		require.NoError(t, err)
   253		require.Equal(t, "origin", elected.Name)
   254	
   255		// A second remote appears after the first election cached the list. Without
   256		// invalidation the election would keep answering from the stale snapshot.
   257		testutil.AddRemote(t, dir, "fork", "https://example.com/fork.git")
   258		InvalidateGitRemoteCache(ctx)
   259	
   260		assert.True(t, isConfiguredRemote(ctx, "fork"),
   261			"a remote added after invalidation must be visible to the election")
   262	}

name: unslop
user-invocable: true
disable-model-invocation: false
description: Cut AI tells from any writing -- filler, hedging, formatting tics. Use when the user says "unslop this", asks to remove AI-sounding phrasing, or asks for writing to sound human.
